title: Coins and Trade
objective: After this level you can explain how Greek cities began minting coins.
summary: Coins began in Lydia; Greek cities then minted their own, each with its own emblem, and the obol and drachma recall older spit-money.

cards.headline: Greek pocket change started out as kitchen skewers.
cards.body: Before coins, Greeks used metal spits as money. Here’s how cities went from skewers to silver stamped with their own badges.

cards.headline: Born next door
cards.body: The first coins were made in Lydia, in Asia Minor, in the second half of the 7th century BCE. They were electrum, a mix of gold and silver. Remember Level 13’s tyrant, a word probably borrowed from Lydian? Money came from the same neighborhood. A lump of precious metal with an official stamp: simple, portable, and nothing to roast.

cards.headline: Skewers and handfuls
cards.body: The names remember what came before. The small coin called an obol takes its name from obelos, “spit”. Six obols made a drachma, a name that probably meant “a handful”, from a Greek word for grasp. So a drachma was, originally, a fistful of skewers. Your pocket change once doubled as a barbecue set.

cards.headline: Money as a flag
cards.body: Each city-state stamped its own identity on its coins. Aegina’s silver showed a sea turtle, a symbol of its naval strength. Athens’ “owls” were struck from Laurium silver and circulated throughout the Classical world. Aegina’s later coins show a land tortoise, which the Art Institute of Chicago reads as sea power lost to Athens. And in Athens, public slaves checked that coins were genuine.
